name: Mewing

lead: Mewing is a posture habit: the whole tongue rests against the roof of the mouth, lips sealed, teeth lightly together, breathing through the nose. People do it for a more defined jawline, a more forward midface and a stronger side profile. It is named after British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, and it spread through social media from 2019.

The idea is that the tongue's resting pressure guides upper-jaw growth forward, with the biggest effects claimed for people who start in childhood. Some users also say the posture lifts the area under the chin and tightens the jaw-neck line. The American Association of Orthodontists has stated there is no evidence it reshapes the jaw, and a 2019 commentary in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery said it is not an alternative to orthognathic surgery. The one controlled study usually cited was a small twin study of orthotropic appliances rather than tongue posture alone.

paras: People practise it as an all-day background habit rather than a workout: tongue up, lips closed, nose breathing, often paired with good head and neck posture, chewing and fat loss for a leaner lower face. Users typically report tracking progress with side-profile photos over months to years.

Gentle tongue posture is not documented to carry serious risks, though some online posts describe masseter enlargement or jaw tension from forceful versions. Orthodontic organizations warn it should not replace assessment for real bite or jaw problems. Mike Mew was struck off the UK dental register in 2024 over his clinical practice, which is separate from the home technique.

angle.text: Mewing aims at a more defined jawline, forward midface and better profile by keeping the tongue pressed to the palate with nasal breathing, an approach drawn from the orthotropics ideas of John and Mike Mew. Users report changes in side-profile photos; orthodontic bodies say tongue posture has not been shown to reshape adult facial bone.

lead: Mewing is a self-directed practice in which a person rests the whole tongue against the roof of the mouth, keeps the lips sealed and the teeth lightly together, and breathes through the nose, with the stated aim of improving jaw and facial structure [1][2][3]. People who practise it do so to work toward a more defined jawline, a more forward upper jaw, better-looking facial profile and a stronger-looking neck-and-chin line, and many pair it with chewing, posture work and, for some, orthodontic palate expansion [4][5].

The term comes from John Mew (1928-2025), a British orthodontist, and his son Mike Mew, who promoted a system called orthotropics. Orthotropics holds that the resting posture of the tongue, lips and jaws during childhood guides how the face grows, and that crooked teeth and recessed jaws are largely postural rather than genetic [2][3]. John Mew traced the idea to a 1958 proposal he called the Tropic Premise [2]. Mainstream orthodontic organisations take a different view of facial growth, and Wikipedia describes mewing as an unproven technique [3].

Interest in mewing rose sharply from January 2019, driven by YouTube, then TikTok and looksmaxxing forums, and it became one of the most recognisable practices in appearance culture [3][6]. The American Association of Orthodontists (AAO) acknowledges that tongue posture plays a role in facial development, while stating that no current research shows the technique benefits the jawline [7][8]. A 2019 commentary in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery examined it as a possible alternative to orthognathic surgery [9]. The practice is also the subject of a long regulatory history involving both Mews, covered below [2][6][10].

paras: The technique is usually described as pressing the full length of the tongue, including the back third, flat against the palate, with the lips closed, the teeth lightly touching or close together without clenching, and attention to nasal breathing and neck posture [1][3]. Proponents describe it as a resting posture held throughout the day rather than a timed exercise. John Mew summarised the posture in the phrase "stand up straight and shut your mouth" [2].

Online communities distinguish ordinary mewing from 'hard mewing', in which people press the tongue upward with more force, and from combinations with other practices such as chewing hard foods, chin tucks and mouth taping. Some forum users pair it with palate expansion by an orthodontist, treating mewing as a maintenance habit around a clinical expander [4]. Proponents also describe the posture as improving nasal breathing and the look of the neck and chin line, claims discussed in the culture section below [11].

Orthotropics claims that the face grows in the direction it is 'guided' to, and that the resting position of the tongue, lips and jaws during development steers the upper jaw forward and outward rather than downward and back. Mainstream orthodontics mainly attributes crooked teeth and jaw form to genetics and growth, and the two views have long been in open disagreement [2].

Clinically, orthotropics has used appliances as well as posture. The Biobloc system combined a palate-expanding appliance with a postural appliance. Other elements include dietary change and training a specific tongue position [2]. John Mew met the German orthodontist Rolf Fränkel in East Germany in 1968, and his account of breathing and facial growth drew on Konstantin Buteyko's work [2]. In a 2022-era YouTube context reported by trade press, Mike Mew also claimed that creating enough tongue space can influence facial growth, including 'expansion of the brain' [6].

John Roland Chandley Mew was born on 7 September 1928 in Royal Tunbridge Wells, began dental training at University College London in 1948 and qualified in 1953, later gaining a specialty in orthognathic surgery at Queen Victoria Hospital, East Grinstead, in 1956 [2]. In 1958 he proposed the Tropic Premise, which treats malocclusion as a postural problem that early intervention can prevent [2]. He practised for about three decades and helped found the International Association of Facial Growth Guidance in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1987 [2].

He also raced cars in the 1950s and 1960s and built a moated castle in Sussex in the 1990s, details that recur in media portraits of the family [2]. Grokipedia traces related ideas to early twentieth-century myofunctional therapy and the London School of Facial Orthotropics, founded in 1983 [1].

Mew's views drew opposition from mainstream British orthodontists. In the 1980s he was fined by the NHS for inappropriate treatment; he appealed to the High Court in 1987, where the judge called the criticisms wholly unwarranted and ruled in his favour [2]. The General Dental Council (GDC) reprimanded him in 2010 over advertisements containing misleading claims, including claims denigrating orthodontics; he did not dispute the charge and described himself as a whistleblower. The GDC revoked his registration in 2017 over false advertising and breach of patient confidentiality [2]. He died on 25 June 2025 aged 96 [2].

Mike Mew promoted tongue posture to a wide online audience, and the term 'mewing' came into use in online communities during the 2010s [1]. Google search interest began rising in January 2019; The Guardian covered mewing as a YouTube face-shaping craze in March 2019, and in 2020 the New York Times Magazine profiled the Mews and their links to incel communities [3]. Influencers posting how-to videos drew hundreds of millions of views, according to Discover magazine, and TikTok searches reportedly passed 4.7 billion [8][6]. Mike Mew appeared on the British television programme This Morning, per Wikipedia's account of John Mew [2].

The practice spread particularly within looksmaxxing and incel subcultures, and by 2023 it had become a general internet meme, associated with 'brain rot' humour and with the character of the Rizzler [3]. The British Orthodontic Society expelled Mike Mew around 2018 to 2019 for continuing to promote orthotropic positions, and he launched a petition against the decision [3][2].

On 6 November 2024 the GDC's Professional Conduct Committee, sitting through the Dental Professionals Hearings Service, found Mike Mew's fitness to practise impaired by misconduct and erased him from the Dentists' Register [10][6]. The charges concerned orthotropic treatment of two child patients between 2013 and 2019 and claims made to parents and in a 2017 YouTube video. The GDC said his approaches were not sufficiently supported by scientific evidence and liable to cause harm, and that he made misleading statements about the need for treatment [10][6]. One patient, a boy aged six in 2018, was reported to have had prolonged seizure-like episodes after extended use of head and neck gear [6].

Mew compared the GDC's position to the Church's case against Galileo and said the regulator was more concerned with protecting the orthodontic industry than children [6]. He appealed to the High Court. In a judgment dated 15 May 2026, the court dismissed his grounds relating to expert evidence and the committee's findings, described the committee's conclusions as unassailable, and noted that orthotropics itself was not on trial, the charges being about his conduct toward two patients. The judgment records that he accepted orthotropics lacks a substantial evidence base [10].
No controlled trial has tested tongue posture alone, as practised in mewing, for changing facial structure.

A small controlled study of 12 identical twins compared fixed orthodontic appliances with orthotropic (growth guidance) treatment without fixed appliances, assessed ten years later by 12 lay judges. Most conventionally treated twins were judged less attractive after treatment, while most orthotropically treated twins were judged improved, and the traditionally treated cases relapsed more often [12]. The study examined professionally delivered orthotropic treatment, not self-directed mewing.

A 2019 commentary in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery examined mewing as an alternative to orthognathic surgery [9], and a 2026 article in the Journal of Clinical Orthodontics discussed the mewing trend [13]. A 1992 paper by an orthodontic author put forward hypotheses that tongue and lip posture influence oropharyngeal development and Eustachian tube function, proposing that early orthotropic treatment might direct growth forward; it reports clinical impressions rather than a controlled trial [14].

The AAO states that tongue posture plays a role in facial development but that changing tongue position alone does not correct misaligned teeth, reshape the jaw or remove the need for orthodontic treatment. Its explainer, published in March 2025, says there is no current research showing the technique benefits the jawline or oral health [7]. AAO president Myron Guymon told Discover magazine that proper tongue posture plays a role in oral health, while mewing 'oversimplifies the complexities of facial structure' [8].

The AAO lists possible downsides of excessive or uneven tongue pressure, including tooth shifting, crowding or gaps, TMJ pain and speech difficulties, and notes that any resulting problems could make later braces more complex [7]. It advises that attempts to move teeth or align jaws be supervised by an orthodontist [7]. Wikipedia reports that most orthodontists do not regard mewing as a viable alternative to jaw surgery [3]. Proponents counter that orthotropics rests on a different view of growth in which posture and breathing shape the face, and that mainstream orthodontics focuses too narrowly on teeth [1]. Discover also cites a 2020 BioScience study reporting jawlines shrinking over recent decades, with researchers suggesting harder chewing as one compensation [8].

Mewing is among the most discussed practices on looksmax.org, with threads from users reporting results, others describing none, and others suggesting it matters mainly in early adolescence [11][15]. Thread titles range from claims that it works with how-to guides to claims that it ruined a face, and others discuss whether it works only in childhood or only under certain conditions [16][17][18][19][20]. A 2025 qualitative study of an online looksmaxxing community analysed 8,072 comments and noted that the community encourages substantial body modification such as mewing and leg lengthening, and argued that participation harms users' health [18].

The word has also become general slang. Some people say 'mewing' in jest or describe a 'mewing face', and students reportedly mew in class to avoid answering questions [3]. Related accessories and terms appear in community threads, such as a 'mewing ring' [21].

Orthodontic palate expansion, which widens the upper jaw with a fixed or removable appliance, is a clinical procedure used to treat narrow palates and some bite problems [22]. Forum users often compare it with mewing, and some report pursuing both [4]. Chewing, chin tucks, mouth taping and myofunctional therapy are other posture and muscle practices frequently listed alongside mewing.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, mewing is treated as a baseline practice that members debate constantly, with advice about age cut-offs, hard mewing, and how it combines with chewing or palate expansion [11][4].
